source.title: Scaling of Wireless Foundation Models via Representation Diversity and Multi-Branch Architectures
source.authors: Ahmed P. Mohamed; Ahmed Aboulfotouh; Hatem Abou-Zeid

record.file_problem: none; the full paper text is present
record.tranche_reason: The paper reports its own wireless-model size sweep and finds that increasing single-objective encoder size gives inconsistent downstream results, including regressions. This bears on V6, but it does not measure language-model pretraining loss or test power-law scaling.
record.gate_note: The paper reports no held-out cross-entropy loss, parameter/token/compute power-law fits, small-run extrapolation, or compute-optimal allocation. Its relevant result is downstream task performance across single-objective encoder sizes, which bears on V6. The fusion and multi-branch results concern objective diversity and architecture, not a single-objective size sweep; cited scaling-law findings are not this study's results.
record.test_reason: The study runs its own single-objective width sweep (256/512/768-d; 6.4M/25.5M/57.1M params) on wireless SSL encoders and reports downstream linear-probe metrics on six tasks. It finds gains on some tasks and regressions on others. This bears on V6 (downstream improvement with scale) in a non-language setting, and the authors argue explicitly that size scaling gives inconsistent returns. It reports no pretraining loss, no power-law fits and no compute allocation, so V1–V5 and V7 are not tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors conclude that increasing single-objective encoder size gave inconsistent and sometimes negative downstream returns with ~25k wireless pretraining samples. They find objective diversity (fusion or a multi-branch model) a more effective use of capacity in that limited-data setting. They attribute the diminishing returns to small, low-diversity corpora, but do not test this.
record.recipe_differences: Wireless self-supervised encoders are compared across hidden dimensions using downstream linear-probe metrics, rather than fitting language-model held-out-loss scaling laws or compute-optimal allocations.
record.method_sensitivity: Downstream results vary by objective and task as encoder dimension increases; the paper reports regressions for RFS accuracy in JEPA and MAE at 768 dimensions and for RFS and jamming accuracy in SimCLR at 512 dimensions.

fits_no_version.finding: At equal 768-d output, three-objective fusion (19.2M params) beats every 768-d single-objective encoder (57.1M) on all six tasks. A zero-overhead multi-branch model (19.2M) beats the best 768-d single encoder on four of six tasks.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Under limited pretraining data, adding objective diversity yields larger downstream gains per parameter than widening a single-objective encoder.

record.problems: The size comparisons cover a limited range of encoder dimensions and a wireless corpus reported as approximately 25,000 samples; they measure downstream probe performance, not pretraining loss, and do not establish a scaling law or behavior over several orders of magnitude. Reported variation is mean ± std over 20 seeds, but the paper does not state significance tests for the size comparisons.
record.rows_left_out: No relevant single-objective size-sweep results from Tables II–IV are omitted. Fusion comparisons in Tables III–IV and multi-branch shared-depth ablations in Table V are not included as rows because they vary objective composition or branch architecture rather than single-objective model scale.

untested.parts: No held-out pretraining loss or power-law relation to parameters, tokens or compute.
No shape-at-fixed-parameter comparison of pretraining loss. The multi-branch shared-depth ablation varies objective layout, not shape of a single-objective LM.
The setting is wireless SSL, but no power-law form is fitted to any loss or metric.

Only three sizes are tested (~9x in parameters), not several orders of magnitude. There is no prediction from pretraining loss, no functional-form fit, no data or compute scaling, and no language-model tasks.
No fitted exponents or fitting-choice analysis.

missing.what: 512-d→768-d single-objective comparisons, which show non-monotonic scaling. Examples: JEPA positioning 1.98→2.08 m, JEPA RFS 81.0→79.9, JEPA jamming 90.8→88.3, MAE RFS 86.5→84.2, SimCLR positioning 2.71→2.77, SimCLR interference 77.4→76.1.

record.verdict_notes: Seed std is given, but no significance tests. Many RFS differences lie within seed std, so the RFS regressions are weak evidence. The size range is narrow (6.4M–57.1M) and only width varies; data and compute are fixed. The paper cites Kaplan et al. only as background.

versions.untested_parts: No held-out pretraining loss or power-law relation to parameter count, tokens, or compute is measured.
No small-run fit or prediction of larger-run pretraining loss is reported.
No compute-budget allocation between parameters and tokens is evaluated.
No comparison measures how architecture shape affects held-out pretraining loss.
The study uses wireless data, but does not test whether a power-law form holds for pretraining loss in another modality or regime.

Tests downstream task performance across a limited set of wireless encoder sizes, but not predictability from pretraining loss, language-model downstream tasks, or scaling over several orders of magnitude.
No fitted scaling exponents, compute-optimal split, or analysis of fitting choices and curve bending is reported.

relationships.condition: Positioning, beam prediction and interference classification, all three objectives, 256→512 and 256→768 width
relationships.reason: Clear gains well beyond seed std, e.g. positioning 2.28→1.76 m (MAE) and interference 75.1→83.6% (JEPA) (r02,r03,r06,r08,r09,r12,r14,r15,r18,r20,r21,r24,r26,r30,r32,r33,r36). JEPA and SimCLR jamming gains (r05,r35) also hold.
relationships.display_finding: Gains exceeded seed variability, including positioning MAE decreasing from 2.28 to 1.76 m and JEPA interference accuracy increasing from 75.1% to 83.6%, alongside JEPA and SimCLR jamming improvements.

relationships.condition: RFS, LoS/NLoS and MAE jamming at larger widths; and the 512→768 step
relationships.reason: Gains are tiny or within seed std (r01,r04,r10,r11,r13,r16,r17,r22,r23,r27,r28,r31). Per Tables III–IV (text, not rows), several metrics worsen from 512 to 768, e.g. JEPA positioning 1.98→2.08 m, so returns are non-monotonic.
relationships.display_finding: Gains were small or within seed standard deviations, and several metrics worsened from width 512 to 768, including JEPA positioning error rising from 1.98 to 2.08 m.

relationships.condition: RFS (JEPA and MAE at 768-d; SimCLR at 512-d) and SimCLR jamming at 512-d
relationships.reason: The larger encoders score lower than the 256-d baseline (r07,r19,r25,r29). The authors state width scaling degrades some tasks, though most drops are about one std.
relationships.display_finding: The specified 768-dimensional and 512-dimensional encoders scored below the 256-dimensional baseline, although most decreases were about one standard deviation.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Single-objective size increases where the measured downstream metric improves (rows r01–r06, r08–r18, and r20–r36)
reader_labels.reason: Many task metrics improve at larger encoder dimensions, including sizable gains in positioning, beam prediction, and interference classification; these results support downstream improvement with scale in those tested conditions.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: RFS for JEPA and MAE at 768 dimensions, and RFS and jamming for SimCLR at 512 dimensions
reader_labels.reason: Larger single-objective encoders regress on these downstream metrics, so improvement is not consistent across objectives and tasks (rows r07, r19, r25, and r29).
